name: Caisson
description:
Caisson is a partially flooded maintenance caisson beneath the western lakeshore infrastructure, accessible only through a service hatch in an abandoned Tier 1 pump station. The space is oval, roughly 40 meters at its widest, with permanent standing water occupying the lower third — a shallow, brackish pool that audiences stand in or around depending on the night's configuration. The ceiling is a dome of riveted steel, the acoustics extraordinary and entirely accidental, creating a natural reverb that sound engineers from the upper tiers have made pilgrimages to study. Maximum capacity is around 150, and the water keeps it from ever feeling anything other than intimate.

Caisson has no fixed booking structure. Shows are announced 48 hours in advance through a single encrypted mesh node, and the lineup is never revealed until the artist begins to play. This policy emerged from necessity — a 2209 raid dispersed a planned event before it started — but has since become the venue's defining aesthetic. The water has risen approximately 12 centimeters since the venue was first used in 2207, and longtime regulars mark the waterline on the wall with chalk after each visit. Notable events include a three-night residency by the Ossian Collective in 2214 that produced recordings later described by critics as 'the most spatially honest music made in Meridian 88 this decade,' and a 2220 incident in which the pump systems partially activated mid-performance, raising the water level by 30 centimeters in 90 seconds before anyone could reach the shutoff.
creator: Origins disputed; most accounts credit an unnamed collective of Shelf sound artists
genre: Experimental acoustic, drone, neural ambient, improvised forms
audience: Experimental music devotees, acoustic researchers, Shelf and Circuit artists, Tier 3 and 4 music journalists seeking underground credibility, sound designers from corporate studios who attend anonymously
cultural_impact: Caisson occupies a unique position in Meridian 88's underground music culture as a space defined entirely by its physical conditions rather than any curatorial vision. The rising water level has given it an unintentional but powerful symbolic weight — the venue is slowly being reclaimed, and everyone who attends knows it. Recordings made at Caisson circulate widely on pirate feeds and have influenced the production aesthetics of several Tier 3 and 4 artists who have never set foot in the space, creating a strange feedback loop between underground authenticity and commercial aspiration.
known_fans: infrastructure workers who maintain the pump systems and look the other way
story_hooks: The chalk waterline marks in Caisson have been rising faster than the water itself — someone has been adding false marks, and the pattern, when mapped, encodes something. A regular notices and doesn't know whether to be curious or afraid.

A Tier 4 sound designer who has attended Caisson anonymously for three years is offered a corporate contract contingent on revealing the venue's location to city infrastructure management. They haven't answered yet.
The 2220 flooding incident was not an accident. Someone reactivated the pump systems deliberately, and the person they were trying to scare was in the audience that night. They're coming back.
